paper_summary: Ukrainian-language master's thesis (National University of Shipbuilding, Mykolaiv, 2023) on the finite-element stress-strain analysis of buoyancy blocks made of syntactic foam (spheroplastic) containing hollow technical-porcelain ceramic macrospheres, for deep-sea vehicles. Chapters 1-2 review buoyancy materials, ceramic hollow-sphere fillers, packing schemes (volume filling coefficients 0.523 cubic to 0.741 hexagonal) and manufacturing routes (casting vs vacuum injection). Chapters 3-4 use ANSYS Student to compute principal stresses in a 100 mm diameter porcelain shell (wall thickness varied 0.25-1.5 mm) embedded with bonded (adhesive) contact in a 300x300 mm syntactic-foam cube under 1 MPa external hydrostatic pressure (equivalent to 100 m depth), varying the distance from the free surface (0.1-40 mm) and the gap between two neighbouring shells (0.2-80 mm). Conclusions: stress concentrations in the foam reach ~30 units near the surface and up to ~3.5 units between close spheres; shells must be buried at least ~15 mm from the surface and spaced at least ~15 mm apart, so bonded (adhesive) contact between ceramic macrospheres and syntactic foam is judged irrational compared with leaving a water-connected gap.

Table 3.1 fixes the single values used in the FEM model, recorded here. The thesis assignment sheet specifies an epoxy spheroplastic mass of density 700 kg/m3. structure.microstructure_notes: Single macrosphere near a free surface (Ch. 3, distance to surface 0.1-40 mm) and two neighbouring macrospheres (Ch. 4, gap 0.2-80 mm), bonded (adhesive) contact, symmetry planes, tetrahedral mesh in the foam and hexahedral mesh in the shell, ANSYS Student. Packing volume-filling coefficients quoted for reference: cubic 0.523, orthorhombic 0.605, double cubic 0.74, double rhombic 0.693, hexagonal 0.741; free pouring gives about 0.6.

test.specimen_notes: External hydrostatic pressure of 1 MPa applied to the cube faces (stated to correspond to 100 m depth); unit pressure chosen so results are dimensionless stress-concentration factors. All numerical results are presented only as ANSYS contour plots and x-y graphs, so no individual stress values are stated in text or tables.

Зовнішні навантаження представляють собою зовнішній гідростатичний тиск, який прикладений до усіх граней куба. (Тиск 1 мПа це занурення на глибину 100 м)

Концентрації напружень у масиві сферопластика у полюсі досить значні і досягають 30 одиниць в дослідженому діапазоні. ... при контакті сфер виникають концентрації напружень приблизно від 1,6 до 4,5 для тонких оболонок і від 1 до 1,8 для товстостінних.

extraction_notes: Ukrainian master's thesis; 'сферопластик' (spheroplastic) is the Ukrainian term for syntactic foam, so the paper is on-topic (hollow-particle composite), but it is a finite-element modelling study rather than an experimental one and contains very little tabulated quantitative property data. Only two tables carry material properties: Table 1.1 (general ranges) and Table 3.1 (single values used as FEM inputs). Record 1 uses Table 3.1 (density 600 kg/m3 -> 0.6 g/cm3, compressive strength 60 MPa, modulus 7 GPa -> 7000 MPa) because those are unambiguous single numbers; the Table 1.1 ranges (600-800 kg/m3, 60-80 MPa, 6-8 GPa) and the 700 kg/m3 density quoted on the assignment sheet are recorded in microstructure_notes rather than as invented midpoints. These constants were neither measured nor computed by the author and no source is cited, so data_origin is 'secondary' with the absence of a citation flagged here. Porcelain shell constants (2500 kg/m3, 410 MPa compressive strength, 60 GPa modulus in Table 3.1; 2400 kg/m3, 400-600 MPa, 60-70 GPa in Table 1.1) are constituent, not composite, values and so are kept in text fields, not as records. Record 2 documents the modelled composite; note that the filler is a 100 mm macrosphere, so particle_mean_diameter_um = 100000 um is correct but is orders of magnitude larger than the usual microballoon and should not be mixed with microsphere data. All FEM outputs (minimum and maximum principal stress in the shell, minimum principal stress and stress intensity in the foam, versus shell thickness, distance to surface and inter-sphere gap) are shown only as figures (Figs. 3.9-3.20, 4.3-4.10); the loading is a unit pressure so the results are dimensionless concentration factors, and no numeric stress value is stated in text or a table apart from the summary statements 'up to 30 units' near the free surface, '1.6 to 4.5 for thin shells and 1 to 1.8 for thick-walled shells' between contacting spheres, '3.5 units worst / 0.8 units best' between spheres, and a loss of load-bearing capacity of about 5x when shells touch. Those are concentration factors with no schema field, so they are kept in evidence/notes and no property value was read off a plot. Other numbers in the review chapter that were not turned into records because they are quoted from other works or are generic: water absorption 0.74-0.75% for epoxy/glass-sphere composites (ref [10]), specific buoyancy of spheroplastics 3300-4500 N/m3, typical microsphere diameters 50-200 um, packing volume-filling coefficients 0.523-0.741 (Table 2.1, ref [3]), depth limits for various shell materials (titanium 3000 m, thermoplastics 1000 m, GRP 4000 m, ceramics up to 5000-11000 m), and a rule that spheroplastic collapse pressure is set 1.5x above the service depth pressure.
